stem: Which two subatomic particles are found inside the nucleus of an atom?
explanation: The nucleus, the dense central core of the atom, contains protons (positively charged) and neutrons (neutral, no charge). Electrons are negatively charged particles that exist outside the nucleus, in the surrounding electron cloud/shells, not within it.
hints: Recall which particle type is missing from the dense, central part of the atom, and which two are found there together.
Electrons are located outside the nucleus, not inside it.

stem: An atom of silicon has 14 protons. One isotope of silicon has a mass number of 28, and another has a mass number of 30. How many more neutrons does the heavier isotope have compared to the lighter one?
explanation: The lighter isotope (mass number 28) has 28 - 14 = 14 neutrons, while the heavier isotope (mass number 30) has 30 - 14 = 16 neutrons. The difference between them is 16 - 14 = 2 more neutrons in the heavier isotope. Since both isotopes have the identical proton count (14, defining them as silicon), the entire difference in mass number is due to neutrons.
hints: Calculate the number of neutrons in each isotope separately first, using neutrons = mass number - protons.
Since both isotopes have the same number of protons, any difference in mass number is caused entirely by a difference in neutrons.

stem: An ion is represented as Al^3+, where aluminum has an atomic number of 13. How many electrons does this ion contain?
explanation: A neutral aluminum atom has 13 electrons (equal to its 13 protons). The 3+ charge indicates the atom has lost 3 electrons, leaving 13 - 3 = 10 electrons. Choice B gives the neutral atom's electron count, before losing electrons. Choice C incorrectly adds instead of subtracting. Choice D confuses the ion's charge value with its electron count.
hints: Start with the number of electrons in the neutral atom, which equals its atomic number.
A positive charge means electrons were lost — subtract, don't add, the charge number from the neutral electron count.

stem: Element Q is a nonmetal located in Period 3 that has 7 valence electrons and readily gains 1 electron to form a stable, noble-gas-like -1 ion. Based on this description, in which group of the periodic table is element Q most likely located, and which specific Period 3 element does this best describe?
explanation: Elements with 7 valence electrons that readily gain 1 electron to achieve a full outer shell (8 valence electrons, a noble-gas configuration) are the halogens, Group 17; the Period 3 halogen is chlorine (Cl). Group 1 elements have only 1 valence electron and tend to lose it rather than gain 7 more, Group 2 elements have 2 valence electrons, and Group 18 (noble gases) elements already have a full outer shell and do not readily gain or lose electrons at all.
hints: Think about which group's elements are just one electron short of a full, stable outer shell.
The group number for main-group nonmetals is often directly related to the number of valence electrons they have.

stem: Rank the following three elements in order of INCREASING atomic radius, and identify the trend(s) responsible: sodium (Na, Period 3, Group 1), chlorine (Cl, Period 3, Group 17), and potassium (K, Period 4, Group 1).
choices: Cl < Na < K, because atomic radius decreases left-to-right across a period (making Cl smaller than Na) and increases down a group (making K larger than Na)
K < Na < Cl, because atomic radius increases across a period and decreases down a group
Na < Cl < K, because group trends dominate over period trends in every case
All three have approximately the same atomic radius, since they are all located close together on the periodic table
explanation: Atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period (increasing nuclear charge pulls valence electrons inward without adding a new shell), so within Period 3, chlorine (far right, Group 17) has a smaller radius than sodium (far left, Group 1). Atomic radius increases down a group (added electron shells), so potassium (Group 1, Period 4) has a larger radius than sodium (Group 1, Period 3), which sits directly above it. Combining both trends: Cl < Na < K. Choice B reverses both trends, choice C incorrectly claims group trends always dominate universally, and choice D ignores well-established periodic trends entirely.
hints: Compare Na and Cl using the period trend first (same row), then compare Na and K using the group trend (same column).
Radius decreases moving right across a period and increases moving down a group — figure out how Cl, Na, and K relate to each other along both directions.
